findings.title: Second downsize definition silently replaces the width/height overload and breaks its callers
findings.body: This adds a second 'def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})' directly after the existing 'downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})'. In Ruby the later definition replaces the earlier one, so the width/height form no longer exists. Any caller passing five arguments now gets ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments). The diff also deletes the public 'OptimizedImage.dimensions(width, height)' helper and changes the positional signature of 'optimize'; any caller of those breaks too. Keep a single 'downsize' that accepts both forms, or update the existing callers and make the change explicit.

findings.title: Request-controlled 'type' ends up unquoted in a shell command via the tempfile name
findings.body: For API URL uploads, the tempfile is created at line 55 with the name prefix 'discourse-upload-#{type}', where 'type' is the unvalidated params.require(:type) value. The new code passes tempfile.path to OptimizedImage.downsize, and convert_with (optimized_image.rb, around line 161) joins the instructions and runs them through backticks with the path unquoted. A 'type' containing shell metacharacters such as $(...), backticks, or ';' therefore becomes executed shell code. This is reached when an API caller uploads an image by URL that is larger than max_image_size_kb. It needs an API key, but it is still command execution that did not exist before this PR. Validate 'type', and pass arguments to the external process as an argv array (system, Open3) instead of a shell string.

findings.title: Oversized images are uploaded anyway when downsizing fails or stalls
findings.body: The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize up to five times and ignores its return value. convert_with returns false (and swallows exceptions) on any failure, such as a missing binary, an unsupported format, or a corrupt file. After the loop there is no re-check of the size, so an image that is still above max_image_size_kb is passed to Upload.create_for as-is. The site's hard limit is therefore no longer enforced on the server. The input and output are also the same path, so a failed or partially written conversion overwrites the user's file with truncated data, and the next pass works on that damaged file. Check the result of each pass, stop on failure, and reject the upload if it is still over the limit.

findings.title: Client size limit hard-coded to 10 MB, ignoring the per-type site settings
findings.body: The size check used to read Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']. It now uses a constant 10 MB for every upload type, so admin-configured limits for attachments and images are ignored in the browser. Users can attempt uploads the site was configured to reject, and the 'file too large' message reports 10240 KB even when the configured limit is lower. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same problem: it replaced the max_image_size_kb setting with the constant. The 'type' argument is no longer used for the size check at all.

findings.title: URL download cap is now a fixed 10 MB, decoupled from max_image_size_kb
findings.body: The download limit for API URL uploads changed from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes to 10.megabytes. Two consequences. First, non-image files fetched by URL can now be up to 10 MB regardless of the admin's limit. Second, if an admin raises max_image_size_kb above 10 MB, images between 10 MB and the new limit are rejected at download time (the rescue nil turns the failure into a nil tempfile), which is the opposite of what the feature is meant to allow. Derive the download cap from the setting, or justify the constant.

findings.title: Animated-GIF detection depends on the tempfile path, so animated GIFs get flattened
findings.body: The animated branch in optimize is chosen by matching the GIF extension against 'from', which is the request tempfile path. Rack multipart tempfiles are typically created without the original extension, so the check fails for uploaded GIFs even when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. downsize_instructions then uses '#{from}[0]', which keeps only the first frame. The result is that an oversized animated GIF is silently reduced to a still image on upload. Determine animation from the original filename or from the file contents, and pass that decision explicitly.

findings.title: New downsizing behavior and changed limits have no tests, and the PR description is a placeholder
findings.body: The PR adds a server-side loop that rewrites uploaded files, changes the public OptimizedImage downsize/optimize API, and replaces the download and client size limits with constants. No specs were added or updated. The description is just 'Test 1'. Nothing covers an image above the limit being reduced below it, the loop giving up after five attempts, a failed convert, the GIF branch, or the duplicate downsize signature (which a spec calling the width/height form would have caught).

findings.title: Synchronous API uploads run up to five full convert and optimize passes in the request
findings.body: For synchronous API uploads, the request thread now performs up to five ImageMagick conversions, each followed by ImageOptim.optimize_image! (which runs several external optimizers), on an image up to the 10 MB download cap, before responding. Each pass rewrites the whole file. A single pass with a scale factor computed from the size ratio, or moving the reduction into the deferred job, would avoid this cost.
